title: Design Detectability Tradeoffs in Preregistered Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop Evaluations for Natural‑Language→Network Configuration
abstract: We report a preregistered, fully archived paired evaluation (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001; confirmatory N=200 multi‑device intents) that measured the marginal effect of a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop generate–validate–repair pipeline (Batfish as verifier) versus single‑pass LLM generation (declared model: gpt‑5‑mini) for translating natural‑language intents into multi‑device configurations in emulation. The preregistered design used a shared initial LLM candidate for both baseline and guarded branches (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate). In the confirmatory cohort the shared initial candidate was identical to both baseline and guarded raw responses for all 200 confirmatory pairs; the deterministic validator (parsing/normalization, task‑payload constraint checks, Batfish reachability/policy checks) reported validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 for every pair, and no verifier‑guided repair was applied (repair attempts = 0/200). The resulting paired contingency table is n11=200, n10=n01=n00=0; exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000) for the paired difference is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00]. Because the shared‑candidate design intentionally suppresses generation variance between conditions, the confirmatory paired test is uninformative for detecting marginal repair benefits under the observed ceiling effect. Our contribution is (1) an artifact‑grounded statement of this factual outcome (with representative artifact references), (2) an explicit specification of the deterministic validator decision rule used to assign verifier_pass, (3) an analysis of the detectability tradeoff introduced by shared_initial_generation, and (4) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for future preregistered evaluations that would expose marginal verifier utility (e.g., independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model sampling, adversarial task selection, vendor image diversity, and trace‑centered metrics).

sections.introduction: LLM‑based systems have been proposed to translate operator intent into device configuration changes for network operations (NetOps). Prior work argues that closed‑loop workflows that place a formal verifier (e.g., Batfish) in the loop can reduce semantic outages caused by unsafe ordering, reachability violations, or hallucinated commands. We preregistered CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 to measure whether a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline with a formal verifier provides a measurable marginal reduction in critical semantic errors versus single‑pass LLM generation for multi‑device configuration tasks. After execution and analysis of the confirmatory sample (200 paired intents), we observed a deterministic ceiling effect caused by a preregistered design choice (shared_initial_generation) that produced identical baseline and guarded candidates for every confirmatory pair, preventing any verifier‑guided repairs from occurring and making the primary paired test uninformative. The paper reframes the result as a reproducible methodological lesson about detectability in preregistered NetOps experiments and documents artifact‑grounded facts, validator rules, and concrete design recommendations for future work. Our principal contributions are: (C1) a preregistered, archived paired evaluation and its artifact‑grounded outcome; (C2) an explicit deterministic validator specification used to assign verifier_pass; (C3) demonstration and analysis of the detectability tradeoff introduced by shared_initial_generation; and (C4) operational recommendations and experimental contrasts required to test marginal verifier utility in future studies.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys, benchmarks, and architectural proposals document active interest in LLMs and agentic pipelines for NetOps and AIOps and consistently recommend verifier‑assisted workflows to detect reachability and policy violations. Formal verification engines (Batfish and header‑space/SMT derivatives) are widely used to detect many semantic configuration errors and are commonly proposed as validators in generator‑validator pipelines. Executable benchmark efforts and empirical studies show LLM outputs can fail on syntax, ordering, and semantic constraints, motivating generate–validate–repair designs. However, evaluations differ substantially in model sets, generation semantics, task realism, and verifier integration; open questions remain about the marginal value of verifier‑guided repair under controlled, preregistered settings. Our preregistered study situates itself in this literature by supplying an artifact‑anchored negative/result‑of‑design lesson rather than a simple model leaderboard. Representative verified sources used in literature synthesis include Batfish/design discussions and recent closed‑loop benchmark proposals (see cited_record_ids).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and core design. CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was preregistered prior to execution and froze sampling, analysis, timeouts, retry, exclusion, and analysis rules. Confirmatory sampling: N=200 multi‑device intents stratified into three topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. Random seed for intent selection and stratified assignment: 42. The declared LLM was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json) and the pipeline used a shared initial generation semantics: the same single initial LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate) was supplied as the starting point for both the baseline single‑pass path and the guarded verifier‑in‑the‑loop path (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation = false). The guarded pipeline allowed at most one verifier‑guided repair iteration per intent (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Timeouts and missingness rules (model call timeout = 60s, verification timeout = 120s, emulation timeout = 300s) and retry policies followed preregistration.
sections.results: Execution accounting and raw outcomes. Execution completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json). The deterministic validator and scoring rule (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were applied to every episode and produced binary verifier_pass outcomes deterministically from archived validator_trace objects (validation_after.valid and validation_after.violation_count fields). The paired contingency table over confirmatory pairs is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered paired difference estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and resamples = 10,000 is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Shared‑candidate identity and repair attempts. The preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one shared initial LLM candidate per intent that—by design—served as the starting candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions. For all 200 confirmatory pairs the archived shared_initial candidate was identical to both baseline and guarded responses (representative artifacts: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-guarded.txt and the analogous files for other tasks in execution/responses/). Because the shared initial candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator for every confirmatory episode (validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in execution/scoring/*.json), no verifier‑guided repair was invoked in the confirmatory cohort (repair_applied == false for every archived validator_trace; repair attempts = 0/200). Representative difficulty diagnostics. Six archived exemplar tasks (execution/representative_tasks/) yield changed_interface_count = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83, median = 2); required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17, median = 4); dependency_rule_count commonly = 2; difficulty labels in the exemplar set include medium/hard/very_hard. Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination filters flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates and no high n‑gram overlap within the confirmatory N, and no confirmatory episodes were excluded (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; analysis/contamination_summary.csv).
sections.discussion: Why the confirmatory test was uninformative. The shared_initial_generation design intentionally controlled generation variance by fixing the initial LLM candidate across conditions; that reduces variance due to model stochasticity but requires the guarded repair stage to actively modify the shared candidate to produce discordant pairs. In our confirmatory run the shared candidate already passed the deterministic validator for every intent, leaving the guarded branch with no opportunity to apply repairs and rendering the paired McNemar test vacuous: with zero discordant pairs the McNemar p‑value is 1.0 and the bootstrap CI collapses to a point. This outcome is a deterministic artifact of the preregistered design rather than an empirical claim that verifiers are unnecessary. Validator ↔ emulator correspondence and construct validity. The deterministic validator reported validation_after.valid == true and violation_count == 0 in every confirmatory episode, and the archived validator traces include the three ordered checks that define verifier_pass: (1) parsing/normalization to canonical command objects; (2) task‑payload constraint evaluation (required sequence, preserved state, allowed field touches) using the encoded expected_final_state in each task payload; and (3) formal reachability/policy checks executed by Batfish on the emulated topology that translate counterexamples into violation codes. These validator decisions are traceably archived (execution/scoring/*.json and execution/responses/*) and show agreement with the emulation outcomes for the confirmatory cohort. Limitations and threats to validity. Key constraints that limit external generalization include single model family (gpt‑5‑mini only), limited vendor/device diversity (FRRouting and VyOS images only), synthetic deterministic task generation that may not capture operator ambiguity or adversarial phrasing, emulator fidelity limits (containerized Mininet‑style emulation cannot fully reproduce vendor hardware timing or race behavior), and the preregistered detectability tradeoff induced by shared_initial_generation. Operational implication. The absence of an observed marginal verifier effect in this run should not be interpreted as evidence that verifiers lack operational utility; instead it demonstrates that a preregistered design choice can deterministically eliminate the opportunity for a repair stage to act. Recommendations for future preregistered evaluations. To expose marginal verifier utility, future studies should (a) use independent per‑condition generation or multiple independent generations per intent to increase opportunities for a repair to act; (b) evaluate multiple model families and sampling temperatures to capture model heterogeneity; (c) broaden device/vendor diversity or include real‑device testbeds to test verifier fidelity against vendor idiosyncrasies; (d) include adversarial or noisy intent banks to surface failure modes; and (e) adopt trace‑centered metrics (counts of tool calls, counterexample provenance, rollback correctness, and iteration‑wise pass probabilities) in addition to final binary pass/fail. Practical notes on reproducibility. All raw responses, validator traces, task manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied evidence bundle (execution/ and analysis/ paths). The confirmatory contingency table and condition summaries are available as analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv, and representative response and validator_trace files are located under execution/responses/ and execution/scoring/ for per‑task inspection.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a bounded verifier‑in‑the‑loop generate–validate–repair pipeline versus single‑pass LLM generation for NL→config translation in emulated multi‑device networks. The preregistered shared_initial_generation design produced identical baseline and guarded candidates for every confirmatory pair (200/200), every confirmatory candidate passed the deterministic validator, and no repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0/200). Consequently the preregistered paired McNemar test is uninformative for marginal repair detection in this cohort (n11=200; n10=n01=n00=0; p=1.0; paired difference=0.00; 95% bootstrap CI=[0.00,0.00]). The scientific value of the run is a reproducible methodological lesson: preregistered generation semantics materially affect the detectability of verifier effects. Future preregistered evaluations seeking to quantify marginal verifier utility must select generation semantics and task/model regimes that create realistic opportunities for verification and repair to act, broaden model and device diversity, and adopt trace‑centered evaluation metrics that capture repair activity and provenance as first‑order outcomes.

Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish used as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The deterministic validator assigns verifier_pass when the archived validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the validator_trace (this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests as described in Methods and recorded in execution/scoring/*.json). The confirmatory run used shared_initial_generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and produced the observed detectability tradeoff. All orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (see execution/ and analysis/ paths in the bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across model families or sampling regimes.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images); verifier fidelity versus vendor-specific idiosyncrasies is untested here.
Synthetic deterministic task generation: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully capture hardware timing, race conditions, or vendor CLI quirks present in production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: the preregistered shared_initial_generation choice reduced generation variance but also reduced sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits—a principal internal‑validity limitation for the confirmatory question.
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the deterministic validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting the confirmatory test's informativeness.
Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks reported no exact duplicates in the confirmatory N, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios (adversarial prompts, retrieval poisoning, adversarial telemetry) were not evaluated and remain important open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
